title: Makar Sankranti (kites; the sun turns)
hook: a small sesame sweet pressed into your palm, and a line that comes with it: take this, and speak sweetly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Makar Sankranti from the rooftops: the sun crossing into Makara, Bhishma waiting for the turn, a sky full of kites. Did you look up? Today, the same day, from the kitchen and the riverbank. Day one hundred fifty-two.

In Maharashtra on Sankranti, people go visiting with a little box of sweets: tiny hard balls of sesame and jaggery, the dark unrefined sugar. You hand one to your neighbor, and you say the line that goes with it: til-gul ghya, god god bola. Take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. It's a small thing, but it carries a lot. Maybe you and that neighbor had words over the parking this year. Maybe your aunt said something at the wedding. The sweet is a reset. Today: what Sankranti is like on the ground, the sesame, the river, and the giving.
screen: `A LITTLE BOX OF SESAME SWEETS.` → `TAKE THIS, AND SPEAK SWEETLY.` → `A RESET.`

segments.voice: Three things turn up again and again on this day. The first is sesame. Til, in Hindi. In the cold of January, sesame and jaggery are thought of as warming, heavy, good winter food, and on this day they become sweets, laddus, brittle, little balls handed from house to house. And they come with words. Sesame is small and sticks together; jaggery is sweet. So the sweet is a promise about your speech for the year. The second is the river. People bathe at dawn on Sankranti, in the Ganga if they can, or in any river, or just at home before sunrise. At Ganga Sagar, where the Ganga meets the sea in Bengal, huge crowds gather to bathe on this day. Water in winter at dawn is cold, and that's part of it: a clean start as the sun turns. The third is giving. Dana, a gift given freely. Sankranti is one of the days when giving is said to count most: sesame, blankets, grain, food for someone who needs it. And then there's the surprise: the same day has many names. In Punjab, the night before, it's Lohri, with bonfires. In Assam, Bhogali Bihu, a harvest feast. In parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, people eat khichdi, rice and lentils cooked together, and some even call the day Khichdi. In Tamil Nadu, it's Pongal, and that's tomorrow. One sun, crossing once, and each place meets it with its own food and its own words. Underneath, the pattern holds: something sweet, something clean, something given.
screen: `SESAME AND JAGGERY: SWEET WORDS.` · `A COLD RIVER AT DAWN.` · `DANA: A GIFT GIVEN FREELY.` · `ONE SUN, MANY NAMES.` · then, large: `SWEET, CLEAN, GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hand someone a sweet. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you've had sharp words with this year. Small or big. Picture walking up to their door with a little box. You open it. You press one sesame sweet into their palm. You don't make a speech. You just say it: take this, and let's speak sweetly. Watch their face. Maybe it softens, maybe it doesn't. That part isn't yours. Your part is the sweet and the words. Breathe there for a while. The bell holds the time.
Makar Sankranti. The sun's crossing, kept with sesame and sweet words, a cold river at dawn, and a gift given freely.
Your line: Makar Sankranti, kites, the sun turns. Today, give one thing freely, and say one sweet word to someone you've been short with. Day one hundred fifty-two.
